Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A gray tabby cat asleep, curled on a yellow knitted blanket on a wooden windowsill, against a blue wall beside a white window with trees outside

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

21 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: The cat's sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white muzzle by the paws Light: Daylight comes through the window on the upper left, lighting the left side of the cat, the top of the blanket roll and patches of the sill.How this lesson was made

What you need

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the pale sky in the windowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat brush: Dab the green leaves outsideOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the white frameFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch flat: Shade the frame lavenderFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Press in the dark stitchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: Press in the light stitchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Block in the curled catFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch angle: Pull the dark tabby stripesAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • #4 round: Paint the pink inside the earsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • small fan brush: Flick the light furFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • liner: Line the closed eyesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #2 round: Press in the pink noseRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Before you start

You are about to paint a gray tabby cat fast asleep, curled on a chunky yellow blanket on a sunny windowsill. The heart of it is the sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white muzzle by the paws. Keep it warm and soft, and let the cat feel cozy.

The light

Daylight comes in through the window. It brightens the cat's face and the near end of the blanket, throws peach sun patches across the sill, and leaves the cat's far end and back in shadow.

What this painting teaches

  • Building from pieces (steps 5, 6, 7, 10, 13). You build a shape from simple pieces: one rectangle or oval first, then curved or straight pieces added on. It makes the frame, the sill, the blanket roll and the whole cat. Leave the pieces showing unless the shape needs to look smooth.
  • Press and lift (steps 11, 12, 17, 20). Touch the tip down, press so the brush spreads, then pull and lift so the mark ends in a point. It makes every knit stitch on the blanket, the pink in the ears and the tiny nose. Too much paint or a slow lift gives a blob instead of a teardrop.
  • Dry brush (steps 8, 9). Only the tip goes in the paint, with no water, and you skim the canvas lightly. It gives the sill its broken shadows and its glowing sun patch. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

The way there

We paint from the back of the scene to the front. First comes the view through the window and the blue wall, then the white frame and the wooden sill, so the room is finished before anything sits in it. Next the blanket goes on as a flat roll, and its knit stitches are pressed in dark, then light. The cat goes on last, over everything: a flat gray shape, its shading and white patches, then its stripes, ears and fur. The lesson ends on the sleeping face, with the eyes, the nose and the whiskers. Early layers leave bare canvas where later stages will cover it, so don't worry about the white you see.

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The white window frame; 2 The yellow knitted blanket; 3 The sleeping tabby cat. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Dabbing, first in step 2.
  • X stroke, first in step 4.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 5.
  • Dry brush, first in step 8. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Press and lift, first in step 11. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 14.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 16.
  • Flicking, first in step 18.
  • Liner work, first in step 19. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The view through the window 3 steps

A soft pale sky and a clump of far leaves, seen through the window.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 3 in tall.

STEP 1 OF 21 · The view through the window, 1 of 3

Blend the pale sky in the window

  • Start: Start at the top left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, the sky through the window.
  • Strokes: Stroke side to side across the corner. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white and paint lower down, then stroke back up over the join a few times while both are wet.
  • Where the paint sits: Keep the blue strongest along the top edge and let it fade to nearly white lower down. The patch's middle is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge and 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
  • Leave: The rest of the canvas stays bare until step 4.
  • Stop when: Stop when the sky is a soft blue-to-white patch in the corner, its lower edge loose and uneven, not a ruled line.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 21 · The view through the window, 2 of 3

Dab the green leaves outside

  • First: Let the sky dry first, or the green will smear into it.
  • Start: Start in the lower part of the pale sky, near the left edge of the canvas, about 2 in from the top edge.
  • Strokes: Wipe most of the paint off the brush, then tap with its tip. Tap the middle of the clump more times so it gets solid, and fewer taps at its rim.
  • Where the paint sits: Keep it to one small, ragged clump about 1 1/4 in wide. These are far leaves outside, so no single leaves, just dappled green.
  • Leave: Leave pale sky showing around the clump and in a few small gaps between the dabs.
  • Stop when: Stop at one soft green clump, solid in the middle and broken at the edges. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

Stroke: Dabbing how to do it, not checked yet

Dabbing also called stippling

Not checked yet

With. round (the tip, for small dots); old stiff brush (for rough patches); a sponge, for soft patches

Load. A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.

Motion. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.

What it leaves. Dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.

Then. Tap a lighter mix on the lit side, leaving the darker taps showing underneath.

Good for. foliage, with an old stiff brush, small dots, with the tip of a round

Tap, don't stroke

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  • A patch went too solid. Tap over it with a lighter or darker mix to break it up.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 21 · The view through the window, 3 of 3

Tap the sunny leaves

  • First: Let the dark green dabs from step 2 dry first.
  • Start: Start on the top of the green clump, the side toward the light.
  • As in step 2: The same tapping as the dark leaves, now with a lighter green and only where the sun hits the clump.
  • Strokes: With a nearly dry brush, tap lightly with the tip, a few taps in each spot so the dots stay broken.
  • Where the paint sits: Put most of the taps on the upper part of the clump where the sun hits, and a couple of small taps lower down in the sky.
  • Leave: Leave the darker green showing under and between the light taps, and the pale sky around them.
  • Stop when: Stop after a few small yellow-green patches. The clump should read as sunny on top and shaded below, not as one flat green.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

The blue wall 1 step

A loose, textured blue wall that fills the room behind the cat.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge.

STEP 4 OF 21 · The blue wall, 1 of 1

Criss-cross the blue wall

  • First: Let the sky and the leaves dry first.
  • Strokes: Use short criss-cross strokes, like overlapping Xs, with Wall blue and some Light wall blue on the brush together, varying how much of each.
  • Where the paint sits: Cover the wall down to a slanted line where the sill will start. Lay a narrow band of Wall blue alone at the inner corner, and run blue down beside and under the sky.
  • Leave: Leave the pale sky and leaves showing. The bottom of the canvas stays bare until step 7.
  • Stop when: Stop when the wall is a loose, textured blue with lighter patches, criss-cross marks showing, and a darker upright strip at the inner corner.

The window frame 2 steps

A white window frame that looks deep, with lavender shadows on its shaded faces.

Where: Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 3 in wide and 7 in tall.

STEP 5 OF 21 · The window frame, 1 of 2

Block in the white frame

  • First: Let the blue wall dry first, so the white stays clean.
  • Start: Start with the tall post, a long rectangle from the top edge down, its middle about 1 3/4 in from the left edge.
  • Strokes: Paint each piece as a rectangle with straight pulls along its length: the post, then a crossbar across the window, then the ledge under it.
  • Where the paint sits: The crossbar cuts the window view in two, and the ledge slants down toward the wall's corner. Keep the frame's pieces straight and fairly narrow.
  • Leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two window openings, and the dark blue strip at the inner corner.
  • Stop when: Stop when the frame is flat creamy white with fairly straight edges and no shading.

STEP 6 OF 21 · The window frame, 2 of 2

Shade the frame lavender

  • First: Let the white frame dry first.
  • Start: Start on the face of the post that turns toward the blue wall, from the top edge down.
  • As in step 5: You build from pieces again, but this time as narrow strips with a smaller brush, only on the frame's shaded faces.
  • Strokes: Lay each shadow as a narrow strip with straight pulls along the piece: down the post's side, along the underside of the crossbar, and along the lower edge of the ledge.
  • Where the paint sits: Shade the faces turned away from the window light. The widest shadow runs down the post's side, where it turns toward the blue wall.
  • Leave: Leave the fronts of the post, the crossbar and the ledge creamy white, where the light from the window hits them.
  • Stop when: Stop when the frame has soft lavender strips on its shadow faces, so it looks deep rather than flat.

The wooden sill 3 steps

A wooden sill that the cat's blanket rests on, with shadow and a patch of sunlight.

Where: Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

STEP 7 OF 21 · The wooden sill, 1 of 3

Block in the wooden sill

  • First: Let the wall and the frame dry first.
  • Start: Start along the slanted line where the blue wall stops, and work down.
  • As in step 5: Built from rectangles like the frame, but with the big brush and just two broad pieces: the flat shelf and its front edge.
  • Strokes: Lay the sill as two big pieces: a wide band for its top, then a strip along the bottom edge for its front, pulling the brush side to side across the canvas.
  • Where the paint sits: Cover the whole bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge and down to the bottom edge, in one even rust brown.
  • Leave: Leave the wall, the frame and its ledge untouched, with a clean slanted join where the sill meets them.
  • Stop when: Stop when the bottom of the canvas is a flat rust-brown sill with no shading or sun patches.

STEP 8 OF 21 · The wooden sill, 2 of 3

Darken the sill's front edge

  • First: Let the rust-brown sill dry completely first.
  • Start: Start along the back of the sill where it meets the blue wall, and work toward the right edge of the canvas.
  • Strokes: Dip only the tip, no water, and skim lightly side to side, building the dark in a few light passes.
  • Leave: Leave a slanted patch of plain rust brown on the sill top near the window, where the sun falls, cut by one thin diagonal line.
  • Stop when: Stop when the sill looks streaky and darker, with brown showing through. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded.

Dry brush

Not checked yet

With. flat; old stiff flat (catches the canvas weave best)

Load. Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.

Motion. Light pressure, skimming the surface.

What it leaves. Feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.

Then. Build up in several light passes.

Good for. cloud highlights, grass, wood and fences, highlights on round things

Skim, with almost no paint

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 11 OF 21 · The knitted blanket, 2 of 3

Press in the dark stitches

  • First: Let the flat yellow roll from step 10 dry first.
  • Start: Start at the rounded left end of the roll, on its top row.
  • Strokes: Touch the tip down, press, then pull and lift so each stitch is a small teardrop. Set them in pairs leaning toward each other, like Vs, in rows along the length of the roll.
  • Where the paint sits: Fill the whole roll with rows, following its curve around the left end. Crowd them darker along the fold low on the roll and along its bottom, where the light doesn't reach.
  • Leave: Leave the flat yellow from step 10 showing between all the stitches.
  • Stop when: Stop when the whole roll is covered in rows of dark V stitches, with a clear darker fold line running along its lower part.

STEP 16 OF 21 · The stripes and fur, 1 of 3

Pull the dark tabby stripes

  • First: Let the white patches dry first.
  • Start: Start at the top of the back, near the upright ear, with the first body stripe.

  • Where the paint sits: Wrap stripes across the back and right end, set bars across the tail, and add short marks on the forehead and cheek. Most of it goes on the right side of the cat.
  • Leave: Leave gray between the stripes, and keep the white muzzle, paws and chest patch clean.
  • Stop when: Stop when dark tabby stripes wrap the body, tail and head, thick at the top and thin at the ends.

Basics: Let each layer dry

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Basics: One light direction

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.

STEP 19 OF 21 · The sleeping face, 1 of 3

Stroke: Liner work how to do it, not checked yet

Liner work

Not checked yet

With. liner; small round (the tip)

Load. Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.

Motion. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. For a tapering line, start thick and lighten as you go. Let lines fork in different directions and overlap, and wobble the edges a little.

What it leaves. Thin, flowing lines.

Then. Reload often.

Good for. branches and twigs, thick at the trunk and tapering, fine lines and details

Thin paint, upright brush

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Add water.
  • Lines spread or feather. The paint underneath is still wet. Only paint lines over dry paint.

Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A gray tabby cat curled asleep on a yellow knitted blanket on a windowsill

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: Nothing in the image is outside the scene.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: extend

Left out: nothing; the edges were painted on

Why: The default size closest to the photo's shape; a crop would cut the cat's ear or back, so the scene was extended at the top and bottom.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things, no texture of hundreds of items (busy measured 0.0%), no detail inside big shapes beyond stripes one mark makes, and about 5 parts.

Why: The picture is already beginner-sized.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.0% of the canvas

A gray tabby curled asleep on a yellow knitted blanket on a sunny windowsill. What matters is the cat's round sleeping shape and its stripes; what's hard is the knit, which has to be one repeated stitch mark. The background is a few flat areas, so the time goes on the blanket and the cat.

Subject: A gray tabby cat asleep, curled on a yellow knitted blanket on a wooden windowsill, against a blue wall beside a white window with trees outside
Focal point: The cat's sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose and the white muzzle by the paws
Light: Daylight comes through the window on the upper left, lighting the left side of the cat, the top of the blanket roll and patches of the sill.

What it saw, back to front

  1. The sky through the window
  2. The blue wall
  3. The white window frame
  4. The wooden windowsill
  5. The yellow knitted blanket
  6. The sleeping tabby cat
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

The only technique with version 2 keys, and the picture paints back to front on white canvas.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner.yaml)

It has no version 2 keys, so the pipeline can't plan with it.

How the paint recipes were worked out19 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Where Claude drew diagrams5 steps, free

Read each step as a first-time painter with only its picture and words. Steps that make a shape appear whole, or whose marks follow a structure, get a diagram; the rest are fills, repeated marks, or small shapes the words place. The writer wrote to the pictures where they differ from the plan, so no line was changed.

  • Step 5: Block in the white frame beginner check

    Noticed: Straight pieces whose order and slant aren't obvious from the picture.

    Pieces: The tall post first, then the crossbar, then the slanting sill edge.

  • Step 10: Block in the blanket roll beginner check

    Noticed: A big shape appears whole in one step.

    Pieces: One long low band, then the left end rounded, as the words say (one roll, no ring).

  • Step 13: Block in the curled cat beginner check

    Noticed: An animal appears whole in one step.

    Pieces: The body as one big oval, the head as a circle on the left, then two triangle ears.

  • Step 16: Pull the dark tabby stripes beginner check

    Noticed: Stripes whose placement follows the body's curve.

    Pieces: Short stripes on the forehead, long curves over the back, bands across the tail.

  • Step 19: Line the closed eyes beginner check

    Noticed: Facial features whose placement depends on the head.

    Pieces: The lower eye as a dipping curve, then the upper eye toward the top ear.

What the reviewer caught5 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Text check: paint Step 2: The paint called Leaf green was measured from the pictures as a soft gray-green (#89af9d), lighter than its name says. (left: renaming it would render part of the chain again; build-steps' note.)
  • Text check: chain Step 4: The wall step's picture also paints the leaves and sky in the lower half of the window, which its blues can't; the image model removed them with the wall and didn't put them back, after two more tries. (left: two redos of the wall's render, both the same.)
  • Text check: words Step 4: Every sentence of its start line failed the fact check, so the page leaves that line off. (left: check-text --final took it out.)
  • Text check: words Step 8: Every sentence of its inside line failed the fact check, so the page leaves that line off. (left: check-text --final took it out.)
  • Text check: step Step 20: The nose step changes almost nothing a painter would see (under 0.2% of the canvas). (left: a step that changes almost nothing needs a new plan and chain; build-steps' note.)
